changes.new: ### Extrapolation beyond the training range *Original figure and English source excerpt: Inria, scikit-learn MOOC, [Exercise M5.02](https://github.com/INRIA/scikit-learn-mooc/blob/0cc70c41c640578c28eb7fd38d8c1c19e09c8aa6/python_scripts/trees_sol_02.py), [CC BY 4.0](https://github.com/INRIA/scikit-learn-mooc/blob/0cc70c41c640578c28eb7fd38d8c1c19e09c8aa6/LICENSE). The four-point calculation below is a Bookvar addition.* By extrapolation, we refer to values predicted by a model outside of the range of feature values seen during the training. ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/classical-ml-trees/mooc-tree-linear-extrapolation.png]] *Inria, scikit-learn MOOC, [original comparison](https://inria.github.io/scikit-learn-mooc/python_scripts/trees_sol_02.html). [CC BY 4.0](https://github.com/INRIA/scikit-learn-mooc/blob/0cc70c41c640578c28eb7fd38d8c1c19e09c8aa6/LICENSE). Unchanged course output: flipper length in millimetres and body mass in grams. The blue fitted line continues outside the observed lengths; the orange depth-three tree keeps its outer leaf values. The synthetic input grid is used to show the prediction functions, not to estimate test error.* In one dimension, every input above the largest training value follows the same sequence of rightward comparisons as that largest value. It therefore reaches the same outer leaf. With squared-error leaves, the prediction is the mean target of all training samples in that leaf. It need not equal the target of the single training sample with the largest input. The same argument applies below the smallest training input. For our four-point dataset, the depth-one tree predicts 1.5 at $x=0$ and 5.5 at both $x=5$ and $x=100$. Ordinary least squares fits $\hat y=1.8x-1$, giving predictions $-1$, $8$ and $179$ at those inputs. These are consequences of the fitted functions. The data do not establish that the true relation keeps rising, or that either prediction is accurate outside the observed interval. ```python from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression linear_small = LinearRegression().fit(X_reg, y_reg) outside_x = np.array([[0.], [5.], [100.]]) print(reg.predict(outside_x)) # [1.5, 5.5, 5.5] print(linear_small.predict(outside_x)) # [-1, 8, 179] np.testing.assert_allclose(linear_small.coef_, [1.8]) np.testing.assert_allclose(linear_small.intercept_, -1) ``` For several input features, a new combination of values also reaches one of the existing rectangular leaves. The claim that all out-of-range inputs receive a single constant is specific to each outer interval in the one-dimensional example; a multivariate tree can still split on other coordinates. The course's [regression lesson](https://github.com/INRIA/scikit-learn-mooc/blob/0cc70c41c640578c28eb7fd38d8c1c19e09c8aa6/python_scripts/trees_regression.py) also distinguishes a plotting grid from an evaluation sample. A grid has no measured targets, and its evenly spaced inputs do not reproduce the frequency of observations in deployment. Drawing a smooth line through grid predictions supplies neither missing labels nor a test distribution.

### Branches of different depths

*The following original English passages and figures come from Inria's
scikit-learn MOOC,
[Other hyperparameters in decision trees](https://inria.github.io/scikit-learn-mooc/python_scripts/trees_hyperparameters.html#other-hyperparameters-in-decision-trees),
[CC BY 4.0](https://github.com/INRIA/scikit-learn-mooc/blob/0cc70c41c640578c28eb7fd38d8c1c19e09c8aa6/LICENSE).
The leaf counts and executable check are Bookvar additions.*

We build a dataset where we illustrate this asymmetry. We generate a dataset
composed of 2 subsets: one subset where a clear separation should be found by
the tree and another subset where samples from both classes are mixed. It
implies that a decision tree needs more splits to classify properly samples
from the second subset than from the first subset.

![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/classical-ml-trees/mooc-asymmetric-depth2.png]]

*Inria, scikit-learn MOOC, [original notebook](https://inria.github.io/scikit-learn-mooc/python_scripts/trees_hyperparameters.html#other-hyperparameters-in-decision-trees),
[CC BY 4.0](https://github.com/INRIA/scikit-learn-mooc/blob/0cc70c41c640578c28eb7fd38d8c1c19e09c8aa6/LICENSE).
Original course output, `max_depth=2`. Points and legend identify the two
classes; background colour is the predicted class. The lower-left region
contains both classes. Three other leaves contain only one training class.*

As expected, we see that the blue blob in the lower right and the red blob on
the top are easily separated. However, more splits are required to better
split the blob were both blue and red data points are mixed.

![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/classical-ml-trees/mooc-asymmetric-depth6.png]]

*Inria, scikit-learn MOOC, [original notebook](https://inria.github.io/scikit-learn-mooc/python_scripts/trees_hyperparameters.html#other-hyperparameters-in-decision-trees),
[CC BY 4.0](https://github.com/INRIA/scikit-learn-mooc/blob/0cc70c41c640578c28eb7fd38d8c1c19e09c8aa6/LICENSE).
Original course output on the same 600 points, `max_depth=6`. New boundaries
appear in the mixed region. This is a training-data illustration, not
evidence that depth six improves held-out accuracy.*

As expected, the left branch of the tree continue to grow while no further
splits were done on the right branch. Fixing the `max_depth` parameter would
cut the tree horizontally at a specific level, whether or not it would be more
beneficial that a branch continue growing.

<details>
<summary>Original tree structure: pure leaves at depth two, other paths up to six</summary>

![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/classical-ml-trees/mooc-asymmetric-tree6.png]]

*Inria, scikit-learn MOOC, [original notebook](https://github.com/INRIA/scikit-learn-mooc/blob/0cc70c41c640578c28eb7fd38d8c1c19e09c8aa6/python_scripts/trees_hyperparameters.py),
[CC BY 4.0](https://github.com/INRIA/scikit-learn-mooc/blob/0cc70c41c640578c28eb7fd38d8c1c19e09c8aa6/LICENSE).
Unchanged original tree; open and zoom to read the node labels.
The root tests `Feature #1 <= 1.764`. Three pure depth-two leaves contain
147, 159 and 3 samples. Only the remaining 291-sample region grows deeper.
This is the fitted structure corresponding to the preceding boundary plot.*

</details>

A maximum depth applies to every path, but does not force every path to
reach that depth. Here the pure regions already have zero Gini, so
increasing the limit from two to six leaves them unchanged. The mixed
region still has candidate splits that reduce training impurity.

The course next limits `min_samples_leaf` to 60. This asks a different
question at each candidate split: will both children contain at least
60 training samples? A 100-sample node cannot split into 99 and 1, or
into 50 and 50. A 200-sample node may split into 120 and 80. The limit
does not specify where in the tree these nodes occur.

```python
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs

mixed_x, mixed_y = make_blobs(
    n_samples=300, centers=[[0, 0], [-1, -1]], random_state=0
)
separated_x, separated_y = make_blobs(
    n_samples=300, centers=[[3, 6], [7, 0]], random_state=0
)
asym_X = np.concatenate([mixed_x, separated_x])
asym_y = np.concatenate([mixed_y, separated_y])
asym_models = []
for settings in [{"max_depth": 2}, {"max_depth": 6}, {"min_samples_leaf": 60}]:
    fitted = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0, **settings).fit(asym_X, asym_y)
    leaf_mask = fitted.tree_.children_left == -1
    minimum = fitted.tree_.n_node_samples[leaf_mask].min()
    print(fitted.get_depth(), fitted.get_n_leaves(), minimum)
    asym_models.append(fitted)
# actual depth, number of leaves, smallest leaf:
# 2, 4, 3
# 6, 15, 1
# 4, 7, 60
```

The source figures are preserved published outputs; the numerical check
uses the same data construction with an explicit tree seed. It reproduces
the root threshold and the three pure leaves. None of these counts
selects a hyperparameter for deployment. That selection requires the
cross-validation procedure described above.

## Обрезка уже построенного дерева

The MOOC calls decision trees **non-parametric** because, without a fixed size limit, the number of fitted rules can grow with the training set. A linear model on $d$ inputs always has $d$ weights and an intercept. A tree instead learns a feature and threshold at each internal node, and a prediction at each leaf; adding data can change both their values and how many of them there are. A binary CART tree with $L$ leaves has $L-1$ internal nodes. With $n$ training rows and nonempty leaves, $L\le n$. A depth limit $D$ also gives $L\le2^D$, so a fixed limit caps the tree even as more data arrive. Repeated input rows, pure nodes and other stopping conditions can keep the actual tree smaller. Non-parametric does not mean assumption-free: this CART model still uses axis-aligned thresholds and constant leaf predictions. The terminology and changing number of fitted components are discussed in the MOOC's [classification lesson](https://github.com/INRIA/scikit-learn-mooc/blob/0cc70c41c640578c28eb7fd38d8c1c19e09c8aa6/python_scripts/trees_classification.py).

sourceComparison.language: Licensed course passages kept in original English. Existing Russian text retained; new worked additions in English.
exclusions: Non-parametric does not mean assumption-free. Axis-aligned constant leaves remain the model's structural restriction.
Depth limits permit asymmetric branches; do not require balanced or symmetric trees.
A depth-three outer leaf predicts its mean, not necessarily the target of the single extremal-input sample. Corrected when using the source extrapolation lesson.
Old notebook warning about multiclass predict_proba plotting is not a current API limitation.
Training-data boundary plots do not establish held-out accuracy or optimal depth.
